questions.q: Why does the correlated subquery version typically cost more than the equivalent JOIN version?
options: The subquery re-evaluates once per outer row, while the JOIN computes each category average once
The JOIN version returns different results, so it's not a fair comparison
Correlated subqueries always fail on tables larger than 1000 rows
JOIN cannot use aggregate functions at all
questions.explain: For N rows and M categories, the subquery does roughly N average calculations; the JOIN version does M.

questions.q: In the JOIN rewrite, what role does the CTE play?
options: It pre-computes each category's average once, so the main query only needs to join against that small result
It duplicates the entire Product table
It replaces the need for an ON clause
It has no functional purpose — it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: This mirrors the CTE concept from Chapter 6, applied here for a performance benefit.

questions.q: Is it always true that a JOIN is faster than any equivalent subquery?
options: No — a scalar subquery computing one simple value can be just as fast, and EXISTS/NOT EXISTS often has no better join equivalent
Yes, JOIN is always strictly faster in every single case
No, subqueries are always faster than JOINs
This can never be determined without running the query in production
questions.explain: The correlated-subquery-vs-join cost difference is specific to that pattern, not a universal rule.

questions.q: What does SQL Server's query optimizer sometimes do with a subquery?
options: It may internally rewrite it into a join-like execution plan, rather than executing it exactly as literally written
It always executes every subquery as a literal cursor loop
It refuses to execute subqueries at all
It converts every subquery into a stored procedure
questions.explain: This means syntax alone doesn't always determine actual execution cost — checking the execution plan can be necessary.

questions.q: For which kind of subquery is the join-rewrite performance benefit LEAST relevant?
options: A scalar subquery computing one simple, table-wide value
A correlated subquery inside a WHERE clause
A subquery re-evaluated per outer row
A subquery joining three or more tables
questions.explain: A scalar subquery (Lesson 52) already runs just once, so it doesn't have the same per-row cost problem correlated subqueries have.
